coredata.dc:description: Biocatalytic nanofiltration (NF) membranes incorporated with enzymes show high capacity for micropollutants (MPs) removal. However, there remains significant challenges such as the lack of molecular-level tailoring for skin layer design and effective strategy for enzyme immobilization. In this work, layer-by-layer (LBL) assembly based biocatalytic NF membranes were fabricated for bisphenol (BPA) removal by immobilizing laccase into the skin layer during the LBL polyelectrolytes assembly with controlled crosslinking and immobilization. This strategy enables simultaneous enzyme immobilization and NF skin layer formation. Three laccase immobilization strategies (i.e., post immobilization, post crosslinking, and post crosslinking and immobilization) on skin layer were explored to prepare NF membrane for evaluating BPA removal efficiency. The post immobilization was identified as the optimal strategy, which endowed the biocatalytic NF membrane with a pure water permeability of 10.9 ± 0.4 LMH/bar and MgCl2 rejection of 97.2 ± 0.3% under 2 bar pressure, alongside competitive laccase loading (238.8 ± 3.5 μg/cm2) and laccase activity (0.6 U/cm2). The optimal biocatalytic NF membrane exhibited an improvement in BPA removal of 79.5% under an incubation mode and 92.5% under a full recycling mode. The removal efficiencies were ~240% higher than that of the unmodified LBL membrane and clearly comparable to other reported biocatalytic membranes. This performance was attributed to the synergistic effect of membrane rejection, adsorption and laccase catalysis. The optimal biocatalytic NF membrane was found to be robust after six cycles within 14 days, while maintaining a relatively high BPA removal efficiency and salt rejection. Overall, our results open up a new avenue for enzyme immobilization into the skin layer of membranes for designing high-efficient biocatalytic NF membranes for MPs removal.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Biocatalytic nanofiltration (NF) membranes incorporated with enzymes show high capacity for micropollutants (MPs) removal. However, there remains significant challenges such as the lack of molecular-level tailoring for skin layer design and effective strategy for enzyme immobilization. In this work, layer-by-layer (LBL) assembly based biocatalytic NF membranes were fabricated for bisphenol (BPA) removal by immobilizing laccase into the skin layer during the LBL polyelectrolytes assembly with controlled crosslinking and immobilization. This strategy enables simultaneous enzyme immobilization and NF skin layer formation. Three laccase immobilization strategies (i.e., post immobilization, post crosslinking, and post crosslinking and immobilization) on skin layer were explored to prepare NF membrane for evaluating BPA removal efficiency. The post immobilization was identified as the optimal strategy, which endowed the biocatalytic NF membrane with a pure water permeability of 10.9 ± 0.4 LMH/bar and MgCl2 rejection of 97.2 ± 0.3% under 2 bar pressure, alongside competitive laccase loading (238.8 ± 3.5 μg/cm2) and laccase activity (0.6 U/cm2). The optimal biocatalytic NF membrane exhibited an improvement in BPA removal of 79.5% under an incubation mode and 92.5% under a full recycling mode. The removal efficiencies were ~240% higher than that of the unmodified LBL membrane and clearly comparable to other reported biocatalytic membranes. This performance was attributed to the synergistic effect of membrane rejection, adsorption and laccase catalysis. The optimal biocatalytic NF membrane was found to be robust after six cycles within 14 days, while maintaining a relatively high BPA removal efficiency and salt rejection. Overall, our results open up a new avenue for enzyme immobilization into the skin layer of membranes for designing high-efficient biocatalytic NF membranes for MPs removal.

ce:section.ce:para: The widespread presence of micropollutants (MPs), such as hormones, plasticizers and antibiotics, in various industrial or municipal wastewater streams is an increasing concern for the aquatic environment and public health [1,2]. MPs can potentially pose long-lasting and detrimental effects to human health even at trace concentration [3]. Yet, with the ever-increasing reliance on pharmaceutical and personal care products, the release of MPs into water bodies is projected to increase in the foreseeable future [4]. For instance, it has been estimated that the concentration of phenolic compounds in the discharged wastewaters can be as high as thousands part per million (ppm), depending on the source of industrial discharge [5]. Therefore, effective MPs removal has become a topic of significant interest in water/wastewater treatment and water reclamation.

To date, many treatment methods, such as coagulation-flocculation, advanced oxidation process and membrane technology, have been proposed for MPs removal [6]. Among them, membrane technology is deemed a practicable solution, based on the combined mechanisms of electrostatic interaction, size exclusion, and hydrophobic interaction [7,8]. For example, reverse osmosis (RO) possesses a great retention efficiency for MPs. The retention of MPs with relatively large molecular weight (e.g., carbamazepine and sulfamethoxazole) can reach >75%, while the retention of the nonionic and small molecular weight compounds (e.g., phenol and 4-chlorophenol) ranged between 45 and 60% [9]. Moreover, enabling membrane processes with other physicochemical processes and natural systems have enhanced the capacity of the technology, rendering it a more economical and sustainable option for MPs removal. Despite these advantages, a single membrane process is unable to meet the increasing demand for higher MPs removal efficiency. There is a need for high-performance membranes to bridge this gap. Multifunctional membrane, such as biocatalytic membranes which integrate enzymatic catalysis into membrane separation, has emerged as a potential solution for highly effective MPs removal [10,11].

Typically, biocatalytic membranes are designed with a selective barrier and supportive layer to immobilize enzyme (e.g., laccase, peroxidase). Enzyme immobilization is a critical process to maximize the reuse of enzymes so as to offer optimal biocatalytic productivity and lowest possible enzyme loss. Adsorption, entrapment, and covalent bonding are the main mechanisms to immobilize enzymes onto membrane matrices [12]. Nanofiltration (NF) membranes is an emerging platform for enhanced enzymatic reaction. The ultrathin skin layer of the NF membranes can retain a part of the MPs and prolong the contact time which leads to complete oxidization by the immobilized enzymes. This advantage is obviously presented to directly immobilize enzymes on the skin layer of commercial NF membrane via surface modification. For example, a polydopamine (PDA) based pre-treatment of commercial NF membrane surface had been carried out prior to immobilizing the enzyme by adsorption [13] or/and covalent bonding [12]. Alternatively, ‘reverse filtration’ of enzyme solution integrated with PDA deposition on the membrane support offers another promising strategy for enzyme immobilization [14,15]. Nevertheless, due to the porous structure of the PDA layer, enzyme leakage is still prominent. Moreover, a significant loss in permeability is generally observed, arising from the strong hydrodynamic resistance of inherent skin layer for commercial NF membrane in combination with the additional modification layer immobilizing enzyme. Hence, a higher operation pressure, suggesting extra energy input, is necessary for fulfilling the desired MPs treatment throughput. Therefore, a rationally designed biocatalytic NF membrane is urgently needed to overcome current limitations and maximize enzymatic degradation capacity.

The layer-by-layer (LBL) electrostatic assembly method provides an effective strategy in designing NF membranes with versatile skin layers [16–18]. By alternatively depositing oppositely charged polyelectrolytes on the membrane substrate, a nanoscale skin layer with tailorable surface charge is formed, endowing the NF membrane with highly competitive pure water permeability [19]. The thickness and composition of the LBL based skin layer can also be precisely controlled at molecular scale by simply tuning the deposition conditions. Because of these advantages, LBL based NF membrane has been used for MPs removal by size exclusion and electrostatic interaction [20,21]. For example, without altering the ionic composition of the feed solution, a high MPs rejection (60–80%) was obtained while showing a low salt rejection (<80%) [20]. Recently, the enzyme, laccase, was creatively immobilized on the LBL supported microfiltration (MF) membrane for 2,4,6-trichlorophenol (TCP) degradation [22]. Over 80% TCP degradation was achieved under a convective flow mode. However, enzyme loss during degradation process remains a challenge. Furthermore, the low salt rejections of currently reported LBL based membranes may also restrict their application as biocatalytic NF membrane. To resolve this challenge, chemical crosslinking of LBL based skin layer was used as an effective method. Chemical crosslinkers can react with the amino groups in the polycations of LBL structure, which reduce the pore size of the skin layer. Our group had developed a positively charged hollow fiber NF membrane via a lumen surface LBL deposition, followed by glutaraldehyde (GA) crosslinking [23]. The crosslinked NF membrane exhibited a high divalent cation rejection (~90% for Mg2+ and Ca2+) and pure water permeability (~17 L/m2h·bar) under a low operation pressure of 2 bar. More importantly, GA is a compatible crosslinker that has been widely used for enzyme immobilization [24,25]. These features make it possible to fabricate enzyme-decorated LBL skin layer by simultaneous enzyme immobilization and NF selective layer formation. With rational design, the crosslinked LBL structure may offer multidimensional space and confined micro-environment for enzymatic catalysis, while retaining acceptable enzyme activity and stability for MPs removal. However, few studies reported the design and fabrication of LBL based low pressure biocatalytic NF membrane for MPs removal. Exploring the immobilization mechanism of enzyme on LBL structure and its long-term stability was even rare.

In this work, for the first time, we describe the design and fabrication of a biocatalytic NF membrane with enzyme-decorated crosslinked LBL skin layer, and investigate its potential for the removal of bisphenol (BPA), an endocrine disruptor widely found in aquatic environments [26]. Laccase was chosen as the enzyme of interest due to its high activity on various MPs, including BPA [27]. Different crosslinking-aided laccase immobilization strategies were proposed to explore their effects on the hierarchical structure, surface chemistry and laccase loading/activity of this newly designed membranes. The synergistic BPA removal behavior (i.e., membrane rejection, adsorption, catalysis) of the biocatalytic NF membranes was elucidated. The stability and reusability of the as-prepared membrane were also assessed. As shown in Fig. 1 , the schematic illustration indicates the development of laccase-decorated LBL biocatalytic NF membrane and its BPA removal process. We hope this work could offer new perspective in designing high-performance biocatalytic NF membrane for MPs removal.

Poly (ether sulfone) (PES) hollow fiber substrate was fabricated in-house with a pure water permeability of around 350 L/m2h·bar and the molecular weight cut-off (MWCO) of 75 kDa. Polyelectrolyte solutions containing sodium chloride (NaCl, Merck) as the supporting electrolyte were prepared with poly (allylamine hydrochloride) (PAH, Mw = 120–200 kDa, Sigma Aldrich) and poly (styrenesulfonic acid) sodium salt (PSS, Mw = 500 kDa, Alfa Aesar). Laccase from Trametes versicolour (EC 1.10.3.2, ≥0.5 U/mg) and Bradford reagent were purchased by Sigma-Aldrich. 2,2′-Azino-bis-(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as the substrate for laccase activity assay. Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC, Mw ~389.38 Da) was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Singapore). GA (50% in water) and BPA were also supplied from Sigma-Aldrich. Other reagents that are not mentioned here were obtained from Merck. All chemicals were used as received. Deionized (DI) water was produced by a Milli-Q system (Millipore, USA).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation of biocatalytic NF membrane via different immobilization strategies
ce:section.ce:para: The in-house fabricated PES substrates were immersed in an aqueous solution containing 30 wt % glycerol for at least 24 h. After drying overnight, the treated substrates were potted into a single PTFE module. The effective membrane area is 85 cm2. The LBL deposition at the lumen surface of substrate was carried out using a previously reported procedure with minor modifications [23]. Briefly, the freshly prepared PSS solution (50 mL, 4 g/L with 30 g/L NaCl, original pH) was first circularly introduced throughout the fiber lumen with a peristaltic pump for 5 min. After rinsing with DI water, the PSS-loaded substrate was contacted with the laccase solution (45 mL, 0.8 g/L in 0.1 M phosphate buffer at pH 5.3) for 1 h at 25 °C, followed by another thorough DI water rinsing. Then, the PAH solution (50 mL, 10 g/L with 30 g/L NaCl, original pH) was pumped throughout the PSS/laccase deposited substrate for 5 min. This polyelectrolyte/laccase based LBL deposition procedure was repeated with the same solutions and conditions until a [PSS/laccase/PAH/laccase/PSS] layer was constructed. With this procedure, laccase was immobilized between the different polyelectrolyte layers. The obtained NF membrane was labelled as LBL-in which indicated the membrane decorated by this inner laccase immobilization process. Afterward, three different capped laccase immobilization strategies were applied for preparing the targeted biocatalytic NF membranes.

Post immobilization (PI) : GA solution (50 mL, 0.1 wt %) was contacted with the lumen surface of the LBL-in membrane for 2 min. After removing the unreacted GA with DI water, the capped laccase immobilization was performed by pumping the laccase solution repeatedly throughout the membrane for 1 h at 25 °C. The obtained biocatalytic NF membrane was labelled as LBL-PI.

Post crosslinking (PC) : The laccase was first immobilized on the lumen surface of LBL-in membrane with the aforementioned procedure, followed by the GA crosslinking. This biocatalytic NF membrane was named as LBL-PC.

Post crosslinking and immobilization (PCI) : 0.05 g of the original GA was dropped into the laccase solution under intense agitation for a certain time. Then, the mixture solution was pumped repeatedly throughout the LBL-in membrane for 2 min to induce a synergistic crosslinking and laccase immobilization. This biocatalytic NF membrane was referred to as LBL-PCI. The overall fabrication procedure for different biocatalytic NF membranes has been illustrated in Fig. A1.

For comparison, LBL deposited NF membrane was also fabricated without inner and capped laccase immobilization, which was labelled as LBL. All the modified membranes were washed by DI water and stored in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 5.3) at 4 °C for subsequent characterization and tests.

The laccase distribution on the lumen surface of the fabricated biocatalytic NF membranes was analyzed by confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM, Zeiss, model LSM710, Germany). The membrane samples were stained with the FITC solution (10 μL, 10 g/L) as reported in a previous work [28]. The morphologies of the membranes were observed by a field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM, JSM-7600F JOEL, Japan) and an atomic force microscope (AFM, XE-100, Park Systems, Korea) operated under non-contact mode. Contact angle measurements were conducted using a goniometer (OCA, Data Physics Instruments GmbH, Singapore). The charge properties of the different membranes were measured by the SurPASS™ 3 Anton Paar analyzer (Austria). The bonding involved in laccase immobilization on the lumen surface was surveyed by an X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, AXIS Supra, Kratos Analytical, UK) with a monochromatic Al Kα excitation source.

Laccase activity was determined by monitoring the oxidation rate of ABTS to ABTS+ [29]. The biocatalytic NF membrane with 2 cm2 surface area was immersed into a 20 mL ABTS solution (0.5 mM ABTS in pH 3 phosphate-citrate buffer solution). The absorbance at 420 nm was recorded at 25 °C over 3 min using the above-mentioned UV–vis spectrophotometry. One unit (U) of laccase activity was defined as the amount of laccase forming 1 mmol of ABTS+ per minute. At least three samples were tested with different membranes, and an average value was taken.

The performances of developed biocatalytic NF membranes were elucidated with a bench-scale crossflow setup. In each test, single membrane module with an effective area of 85 cm2 was installed into the setup. The feed solution was always introduced to the membrane lumen side where the inside-out filtration was performed. The pure water permeability, salt permeability (expressed in unit of L/m2h·bar abbreviated as LMH/bar) and salt rejection of the biocatalytic NF membranes were tested in the laminar flow regime at a crossflow velocity of 0.2 m/s under 2 bar pressure. The single salt rejection was conducted with Na2SO4, MgSO4, and MgCl2 solutions at 1000 ppm, based on the conductivity measurement (Ultrameter II, Myron L Company, Canada) of the feed and permeate solutions. The BPA rejection of biocatalytic NF membranes was evaluated with BPA solution (34.2 mg/L in 0.1 M acetate buffer, pH 5.5) at 2 bar pressure under different crossflow velocities (0.1–0.3 m/s). Before the BPA rejection test, the biocatalytic NF membranes were treated with 45 °C HCl solution (pH 3) for 2 h to induce laccase deactivation [30]. The BPA content in the feed and permeate was detected by a high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, Shimadzu, Japan) installed with a UV–visible detector and a C18 HPLC column (Inertsil® ODS-3, 150 mm × 4.6 mm i.d.; 5 μm; GL Sciences, Japan). The detailed testing conditions and protocols followed a previous work [31]. A series of neutral organic solutes such as glycerol, glucose, and sucrose were used to detect the MWCO of the different membranes following the same testing protocols [23,32]. All tests were repeated with five different samples for each type of membrane.

ce:section.ce:section-title: BPA removal by biocatalytic NF membranes

ce:section.ce:para: The contribution of adsorption and laccase catalysis for BPA removal using biocatalytic NF membranes could be quantified with incubation mode. Briefly, BPA solution (50 mL) was cyclically pumped throughout the membrane module with a peristaltic pump at 5 mL/min under 25 °C. 0.25 mL of the sample was taken from the feed tank at regular intervals and mixed immediately with 0.2 mL of 0.1 M HCl for HPLC analysis to determine the remaining BPA concentration. Three parallel samples were tested for each type of membrane.

The full recycling mode was applied to evaluate the BPA removal efficiency of different biocatalytic NF membranes with as described crossflow setup. The BPA solution was added to the feed tank with an effective volume of 5.0 L and pumped throughout the NF membrane module at 2 bar pressure under different crossflow velocities (0.1–0.3 m/s). The NF permeate was recirculated to the feed tank until the samples were collected at regular intervals. The BPA content in the collected permeate was measured using HPLC with the aforementioned protocol. After each run, the setup was cleaned successively with 2% NaOH (40 °C) and 2% HNO3 (40 °C) and abundantly rinsed after each cleaning step with DI water.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Reusability and stability of biocatalytic NF membranes
ce:section.ce:para: The stability and reusability of the biocatalytic NF membranes were investigated by testing the BPA removal efficiency on a daily basis. Continuous filtration of the BPA solution under full recycling mode was performed for 5 h for each day. The operation conditions were as follows: 2 bar operation pressure, 0.2 m/s of crossflow velocity, at 25 ± 0.5 °C temperature. The BPA solution in the feed tank was replenished daily. Once the BPA removal efficiency of the tested biocatalytic NF membrane was below 80%, backwashing with DI water was triggered under a 1.5 bar pressure for 0.5 h. This filtration-backwashing process was defined as one reuse cycle. The evaluation of stability and reusability was based on the reuse cycle number for a single NF membrane module. The entire evaluation process was terminated when the recovered BPA removal efficiency dropped to 80% after backwashing. The BPA permeability of biocatalytic NF membrane was also recorded during the entire filtration process at regular intervals. After DI water rinsing, the MgCl2 rejection and laccase activity of biocatalytic NF membrane were measured. It should be noted that the tested membrane module was thoroughly cleaned with DI water after filtration for a day. The membrane module was stored in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 5.3) overnight at 4 °C for the next test batch. At the same time, another of the same biocatalytic NF membrane was stored in the buffer at 25 ± 0.5 °C without filtration operation. The laccase activity was measured every day to determine the stability of biocatalytic NF membranes. Meanwhile, the laccase concentration in the storage buffer was tested to verify the leakage of laccase from the developed membranes.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Surface structure and property of biocatalytic NF membranes
ce:section.ce:para: The distribution of laccase on the lumen surface of biocatalytic NF membranes was observed by CLSM. As shown in Fig. 2 , laccase-FITC (green) is evenly anchored on the surface of lumen side, especially for LBL-PI membrane, indicating the successful immobilization of laccase. It could be attributed to the good compatibility and chemical bonding between laccase and the polyelectrolytes of the LBL assembly, which will be discussed in the following section.

The chemical bonding in the lumen surface was then explored with a high resolution XPS C 1s and N 1s of LBL NF membrane and biocatalytic NF membranes. As depicted in Fig. 4A1, the C 1s component peak at 288 eV (C=O/C=N) for LBL NF membrane is evident, which can be explained by the formation of C=N bonds due to the crosslinking between the amino groups of PAH and aldehyde groups of GA [23]. Compared with LBL NF membrane, the intensity of C–H/C–C peak at 284.8 eV is stronger than the C–N/C–O peak at 285.9 eV after laccase immobilization for all types of biocatalytic NF membranes. While it is reasonable to see a stronger C–H/C–C intensity as laccase offered more C–C structures over the entire membrane surface, the fluctuation in the intensity of C=O/C=N peak apparently reveals different immobilization mechanisms with different laccase immobilization strategies. Due to the almost neutral or little charge on the membrane surface and laccase at pH 5.3 [14], the noncovalent bonding (e.g., hydrophobic adsorption, hydrogen bonding) dominated the laccase immobilization in LBL structure. For the PI strategy, a nucleophilic attack taken place by the ε-amino groups from lysine of laccase to GA [24], accompanied by the crosslinking between GA and PAH, which induced the covalent bonding (e.g., PAH−N=C−GA, laccase−N=C−GA) in LBL structure. Only the remaining unreacted GA would react with the capped immobilized laccase to form the laccase-N=C-GA structure. Therefore, the intensity of C=O/C=N peak for LBL-PI membrane was weaker than that of LBL membrane (Fig. 4B1). In comparison, Fig. 4C1 exhibited the weakest C=O/C=N intensity. This was attributed to the limited immobilization loading of laccase by the PC strategy. Due to weaker noncovalent bonding between capped laccase and PSS, the amount of laccase that stayed on the membrane surface is obviously reduced after rinsing. This triggers the least amount of laccase−N=C−GA structure after the subsequent GA crosslinking. In contrast, the PCI strategy induces sufficient intermolecular crosslinking between the free laccase molecules and GA, which in turn produces a larger amount of laccase−N=C−GA−C=N−laccase structure. Therefore, more obvious C=N peak was identified on the lumen surface of LBL-PCI membrane after crosslinking with PAH (Fig. 4D1).

The laccase immobilization mechanisms could be further explored by analyzing the high resolution N 1s XPS spectra of membranes. As the covalent bonding agent, GA could change the laccase conformation by consuming its active sites [29]. Compared with other biocatalytic NF membranes, the LBL-PI membrane exhibits a stronger intensity of N–H peak at 401.6 eV (Fig. 4B2), which indicates a surface with PAH−N=C−GA−C=N−laccase structure. Such a structure was beneficial to the higher activity and activity recovery rate [29]. As described above, abundant covalent bonded laccase-laccase structure was produced with the PCI strategy, demonstrating a stable network. However, the N–H peak with the weakest intensity for LBL-PCI membrane (Fig. 4D2) suggests that the natural conformation of laccase has been partially changed by the crosslinking active sites, which predicted the compromised catalytic activity of designed membrane. In summary, the hypothetical mechanisms of different laccase immobilization strategies were illustrated in Fig. A4. Overall, laccase is immobilized on the lumen surface based on either covalent crosslinking with GA or intermolecular crosslinking with other laccase. Such methods of immobilization are likely to minimize the leakage of laccase. Especially for the PCI strategy, there is sufficient intermolecular crosslinking to form a network among laccase molecules, despite some laccase molecules are not directly immobilize on the lumen surface. This helps to stabilize the laccase molecules, preventing them from potential leakages. In the case of the PI strategy, fewer intermolecular crosslinking is formed, which ensures a higher exposure to the MPs. Nevertheless, we speculate that the stability of laccase could still be guaranteed, given covalent crosslinking with GA molecules. This hypothesis may also be well-suited for the PC strategy, which uses a combination of the aforementioned crosslinking types. As mentioned, the only possible drawback of the PC strategy is the limited laccase loading, which will be further explored in the following section. Despite partial GA molecules are consumed for crosslinking PAH in PI strategy, the remaining GA molecules render the laccase with better mobility which in return maximumly expresses the catalytic ability. On the contrary, PCI strategy ensures the stronger bonding for laccase, whereas decreasing its mobility.

As laccase were introduced onto the lumen surface by different immobilization strategies, the surface hydrophilicity and charged property of the respective membranes were altered. As shown in Fig. 5 A, a slightly higher hydrophobicity is observed for the LBL-PI membrane. It could be attributed to the weaker effect of PI process on laccase conformation. Larger hydrophobic surface area (~9895 nm2) on natural laccase molecule has been identified, compared with its hydrophilic part (~7219 nm2) [12]. Although covalent bonded laccase formed, the PI process produced laccase with a higher degree of freedom, which well-preserved its hydrophobicity. The rapid decrease in contact angle over time was also impacted by the amphiphilic property of the laccase molecules, where the hydrophilic part accelerated the spread of water molecules. The zeta potential results also revealed a similar immobilization behavior (Fig. 5B). LBL membrane and biocatalytic NF membranes possessed a positively charged surface, due to the high surface N/S ratio discussed in previously published work [23]. After laccase immobilization with the PI strategy, the isoelectric point of the LBL-PI membrane decreases to pH = 7.5. It could be interpreted by the larger negatively charged surface area (~1237 nm2, roughly 2-fold that of the positively charged surface area) of the laccase molecule [12], which improved the negative charge of obtained membrane. For the PC and PCI strategies, more active sites of the laccase molecules were crosslinked with PAH and GA, thereby consuming more N–H groups and reducing the positively charges of LBL-PC and LBL-PCI membranes.

The effect of different immobilization strategies on the laccase loading is shown in Fig. 6 . The biocatalytic NF membranes exhibit a limited laccase loading (<3.0 mg) and immobilization efficiency (~8%) for inner laccase decoration process, which may due to the noncovalent bonding of laccase with LBL components. Notably, LBL-PI membrane presented the highest laccase loading (20.32 ± 0.28 mg) in capped immobilization process. This indicates that crosslinked lumen surface with free GA molecules was favorable to immobilize laccase, although partial GA molecules have been depleted for crosslinking with laccase from the LBL layers. Combining the amount of immobilized laccase in LBL structure, the PI immobilization strategy endowed the biocatalytic NF membrane with competitive laccase loading (~22.9 mg, i.e., ~269 μg/cm2) and laccase activity (0.59 ± 0.08 U/cm2, not shown in Fig. 6), which was superior to our other immobilization strategies. This is attributed to the fact that the unreacted GA molecules on the lumen surface of LBL-PI membrane provided more ‘anchored sites’ for laccase immobilization by covalent bonding, while maintaining the laccase conformation. For LBL-PCI membrane, despite a relatively higher overall immobilization efficiency (~25%, ~8.7 mg) was confirmed, the intermolecular crosslinking between laccase molecules changed their conformations, resulting in the lowest laccase activity (0.29 ± 0.12 U/cm2). In contrast, PC strategy induced the lowest laccase loading (~5.3 mg), especially in its capped immobilization process. However, the dominant crosslinking between laccase molecules and LBL components retained the partial activity of biocatalytic NF membrane (0.36 ± 0.07 U/cm2). A biocatalytic NF membrane should possess high enzyme activity and loading for desired enzymatic degradation of MPs. In this regard, the PI strategy is the most suitable method for laccase immobilization.

Besides catalytic activity, the NF performances of designed membranes also act the crucial role in influencing the MPs removal. Fig. 7 portrays the permeability and rejection of the LBL and biocatalytic NF membranes against various inorganic salts at 2 bar pressure. LBL membrane indicated a pure water permeability of ~13 L/m2h·bar which was much lower than that of PES substrate (350 L/m2h·bar, as mentioned in Section 2.1), demonstrating the successful LBL deposition. Compared with LBL membrane, a further decrease in pure water permeability was observed for the biocatalytic NF membranes, deriving from the enhanced hydrodynamic resistance by laccase immobilization. This loss in permeability is also observed in previously published work [13,33]. However, the different laccase immobilization strategies induced discriminated NF transport properties. As depicted in Fig. 7A, even though limited permeabilities decline for pure water and salt solutions were identified, LBL-PCI membrane exhibited obviously compromised salt rejection (Fig. 7B). This decline is attributed to the intermolecular crosslinking between laccase molecules (as indicated in XPS results and Fig. A4), causing the subsequent inadequate crosslinking in the LBL structure. The MWCO test also mirrored the same conclusion with a lower neutral solute rejection for LBL-PCI membrane (Table A1). The inadequate crosslinking caused a relatively loose skin layer and higher MWCO (~355.7 Da), thereby compromising its salt rejection. In comparison, the LBL-PI membrane confers a 94 ± 0.4% rejection for MgSO4 and 97.2 ± 0.3% rejection for MgCl2 under 2 bar pressure. Such higher rejections benefit from the well-crosslinked network between the laccase molecules and polycations in PI strategy induced LBL structure. With this tighter skin layer (MWCO of 244.1 Da), the size exclusion effect of biocatalytic NF membrane is significantly enhanced. The size exclusion effect, combined with its positively charged lumen surface as attested by zeta potential results (Fig. 5B), renders the LBL-PI membrane with desirable rejection for divalent cations.

As compared with the NF performances of currently reported LBL based membranes, the as-designed LBL-PI membrane in this work demonstrated the superior perm-selectivity, either in salt permeability or salt rejections, as shown in Table 1 . Especially, this desired NF performance is obtained under a 2 bar operation pressure which is lower than the required pressure (>5 bar) for most commercial NF membranes. Furthermore, LBL deposition and enzyme immobilization proposed in this work is solution processable. The polyelectrolytes and enzyme solutions can also be recycled for producing multiple membrane modules with stable output. These yield a cost advantage over existing fabrication procedures for biocatalytic NF membrane, indicating the potential to reduce energy consumption and chemical use.

For the removal of MPs with commercial NF membrane, size exclusion or electrostatic interaction serves as the main removal mechanism. In the case of BPA (hydrophobic neutral), its nonionic structure confers to an insignificant electrostatic effect by the charged membrane surface [4]. Therefore, size exclusion is the dominant mechanism for BPA removal. However, for the biocatalytic NF membrane, besides rejection (i.e., size exclusion effect), adsorption and enzyme catalysis also contribute towards the BPA removal. Hence, exploring the actual rejection ability against BPA is beneficial to the understanding of the BPA removal process. As listed in Table 2 , the BPA rejection under different crossflow velocities was quantified. Before testing, all types of biocatalytic NF membranes are deactivated without disturbing the laccase-decorated LBL structure. As crossflow velocity increases, a gradual increase in the BPA rejection is detected in the LBL and all biocatalytic NF membranes due to a reduced concentration polarization effect. Expectedly, the LBL-PI membrane shows the highest BPA rejection (>38%) which corresponded to its lowest MWCO (Table A1). A higher BPA rejection will enrich the BPA molecules near the laccase-decorated skin layer, lengthening the reaction time between BPA and laccase. In return, the catalytic efficiency is expected to be improved, making it possible to achieve a sustainable BPA removal, which will be confirmed in the following section. It should be noted that this BPA rejection was far below the theoretical value (~90%) by comparing the molecular weight of BPA (228.3 g/mol) with the MWCO of LBL-PI membrane. It could be ascribed to the synergetic effects of BPA physicochemical properties (i.e., hydrophobic neutral) and membrane surface property (i.e., relatively hydrophobic), which induced the undesired BPA molecules penetration.

As mentioned above, the BPA removal by biocatalytic NF membrane was based on the synergistic membrane rejection, adsorption, as well as laccase catalysis. The contribution by these mechanisms also varies with the different laccase immobilization strategies. Fig. 8 shows the BPA removal efficiency of LBL and biocatalytic NF membranes under incubation mode, which is aroused by the combination of membrane adsorption and laccase catalysis. For LBL membrane, the BPA removal efficiency gradually increases and stabilizes at 23.5% after incubation for 10 h. It could be attributed to the saturated adsorption capacity induced by the accumulation of BPA molecules. With laccase immobilization, the BPA removal difference between LBL membrane and biocatalytic NF membranes is mainly derived from the laccase catalysis, which is about 55.9%, 45.8%, and 42.4% for LBL-PI, LBL-PC, and LBL-PCI membrane, respectively. This outcome is consistent with the laccase loading (Fig. 6) and activity brought by different immobilization strategies. Although the PC strategy resulted in the lowest laccase loading (62.1 μg/cm2), partial activity of laccase was maintained due to the synergistic crosslinking among laccase molecules, PAH and GA, thereby rendering the LBL-PC membrane with around 70% BPA removal. On the other hand, LBL-PI membrane showed the highest BPA removal (~79%), which was much higher than that for LBL-PCI membrane (~65%). First, this was attributed to the superior laccase loading by PI strategy. Second, better mobility of laccase derived from PI strategy secured higher exposure probability to BPA, thus leading to efficient BPA oxidation. In addition, the PI strategy achieved the better distribution of enzyme on lumen surface (Fig. 2), which was more favorable for BPA interaction with laccase.

The superiority of the PI strategy on enzyme immobilization was further evaluated by BPA removal under a full recycling mode. As shown in Fig. 9 , the overall BPA removal efficiency of biocatalytic NF membranes was enhanced with the combination of membrane rejection, adsorption, and laccase catalysis. The BPA removal efficiency of LBL-PI membrane reached over 90%, exceeding that of the LBL-PC and LBL-PCI membranes at ~80% and ~76%, respectively. As mentioned before, it could be ascribed to the higher mobility and loading of laccase molecules as well as their uniform distribution. It was worth mentioning that the contribution of membrane adsorption and laccase catalysis on BPA removal dropped under full recycling mode, as compared with incubation mode. In the case of 0.1 m/s crossflow velocity (Fig. 9A), membrane adsorption and laccase catalysis of LBL-PI membrane conjunctively contributed around 53.5% BPA removal, which is lower than the results under corresponding incubation mode (~79%, see Fig. 8). This proportionate loss can be explained by the shielding effect of crossflow on BPA adsorption and oxidation. The crossflow state of the feed solution may reduce the contact probability between BPA molecules and capped laccase molecules, thus restricting the effects of membrane adsorption and laccase catalysis. Such a phenomenon is more obvious under a higher crossflow velocity. For LBL-PI membrane, the contribution proportion of membrane adsorption and laccase catalysis descended to around 49% when elevating the crossflow velocity to 0.3 m/s, reducing the overall BPA removal efficiency to ~90.3% (Fig. 9A). However, this shielding effect seems negligible for LBL-PC and LBL-PCI membranes. This suggests that the increased rejection contribution on overall BPA removal replenished the proportion loss of membrane adsorption and laccase catalysis. With the above discussion, the crossflow velocity under a full recycling mode does have an influence on the adsorption and catalysis capacities of the newly developed membranes. Even though encouraging BPA removal efficiency was demonstrated under a lower crossflow velocity, especially for LBL-PI membrane, the easy accumulation of BPA molecules and their degradation products may burden the activity sites of laccase, eventually compromising the service duration of the membrane. A higher crossflow velocity also indicates an undesired energy consumption and weakens the effects of laccase activity, which is the primary focus in this work. Therefore, a crossflow velocity of 0.2 m/s is selected for the following exploration.

The variation of BPA removal efficiency with operation time was investigated to gain deeper insight into the effect of different laccase immobilization strategies. For LBL-PI membrane, the BPA removal efficiency significantly increases in the initial filtration process (0–1.5 h, Fig. 9B) and climbs to ~92.5% after 1.5 h. Accordingly, LBL-PCI membrane, which has the lowest BPA removal efficiency, shows 9.4% increase in the initial 2 h of the experiment, bringing its overall BPA removal efficiency to ~76.1%. As aforementioned, a relatively denser skin layer is formed with the LBL-PI membrane, promoting a higher BPA rejection. Under a fixed crossflow velocity, it impelled the rapid accumulation of BPA molecules on the skin layer. Furthermore, the impressive laccase loading and activity of the LBL-PI membrane also synergistically improved the BPA removal efficiency, consequently curtailing the time to reach removal stabilization.

In summary, under dipping incubation mode, membrane adsorption and laccase catalysis of the biocatalytic NF membranes collectively dominate the BPA removal process. Some of the BPA molecules were adsorbed on the lumen surface due to the porous structure of the LBL deposition layer. Under the catalytic activity of the laccase, these BPA molecules were first oxidized to some reactive intermediates (e.g., 4-isopropenylphenol), then to aromatic products (e.g., quinone), before eventually converted to polymers of lower molecular weight (e.g., 4-Methylpent-3-oic acid and hexadecane) [40]. At the same time, the size exclusion effect by the membrane also participated in the removal of BPA under the full recycling mode. As illustrated in Fig. 1, some BPA molecules were entrapped on the lumen surface, based on the synergetic effect of adsorption and size exclusion, and were degraded by the immobilized laccase. Being rejected on the surface of the membrane prolonged the contact time between BPA molecules and laccase, which allowed sufficient time for the surface laccase to work on the BPA molecules and oxidized them. Meanwhile, penetrated BPA molecules could be oxidized by laccase that were immobilized in the LBL deposition layer. In any case, the products of BPA oxidation, with a larger molecular weight, may accumulate in the membrane and on the surface due to the adsorption and size exclusion.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Reusability and stability in BPA removal
ce:section.ce:para: The reusability and stability of designed biocatalytic NF membrane is crucial to the long-term MPs removal under realistic operation conditions. Hence, the long-term performances of LBL-PI membrane on continuous treatment of BPA solution with full recycling mode was explored. As illustrated in Fig. 10 A, the BPA removal rate of LBL-PI membrane decreases to 80% of its initial value after a 5-day operation (total 25 h). This is because of the accumulation of BPA oxidation products on the lumen surface. In the meantime, the catalytic activity of LBL-PI membrane is declined to ~96% (Fig. 10B), due to the steric hindrance of these by-products, which impedes the contact with BPA molecules. Subsequently, backwashing with DI water was proposed to prolong the service duration of the LBL-PI membrane. After the backwashing process, its BPA removal efficiency returns remarkably to ~90%, accompanied by the recovery of the feed water permeability to 8.93 ± 0.04 LMH/bar at the beginning of 2nd cycle (Fig. 10B). It should be noted that LBL-PI membrane still maintained over 99% of the original MgCl2 rejection (Fig. 10B), confirming the well integrity of the laccase based LBL skin layer during the entire filtration-backwashing process. This result was in line with our previous work [41,42], which collectively verified the backwashing tolerance of LBL skin layer. Although the period of filtration-backwashing process was compressed in each cycle, backwashing realizes at least 5% recovery of BPA removal efficiency until the removal efficiency was detected at around 80% of its initial recovery at 6th cycle. Moreover, the catalytic activity of the LBL-PI membrane is retained above 85% of its original value after the 6th cycle. The loss of BPA permeability is also found to be limited within 1.5%.

It is therefore reasonable that the irreversible fouling induced by catalytic oxidation products of MPs is hardly eliminated by a single backwashing, in particular for NF membrane with a relatively dense skin layer. In the case of BPA removal, its oxidation products may penetrate the skin layer and attach in the pore structure of the NF membrane during the long-term operation [14]. Therefore, backwashing at well-designated timeframe will guarantee a desired BPA removal efficiency, while avoiding total irreversible deactivation of immobilized enzyme. With the proposed backwashing schedule in this work, our LBL-PI membrane exhibits a sustainable BPA removal ability (>80%) for 14 days (total 62 h with six cycles), which surpasses the BPA rejection ability of LBL membrane (shown as dash line in Fig. 10A). This performance on reusability was also comparable with other laccase based biocatalytic membranes in the literature (Table 3 ).

As a comparison, the laccase activity retention of different biocatalytic NF membranes was also investigated in a ‘storage buffer’ for 10-day storage. As illustrated in Fig. 11 A, all the developed membranes performed a similar trend in activity attenuation which decreased to ~92%. This is comparable with other reported supports immobilized with enzymes [14,45]. For instance, the activity of laccase-loaded Amberlite beads reduced to 30% after 7-day reuse [45]. Moreover, the overall laccase loading retention was maintained above 95% during a 10-day storage (Fig. 11B), indicating only limited leakage of laccase from the developed membranes. The satisfactory stability of our laccase based LBL biocatalytic NF membranes is mainly due to (1) The confined micro-environment in the lumen side of hollow fiber membrane which evades the negative impact of the external environment on laccase. (2) Covalent bonding that offered the structure stability to the laccase based skin layer. It should be noted that the LBL-PI membrane possessed a relatively more obvious leakage of laccase, which was attributed to the presence of residual laccase that was not crosslinked via the GA molecules. Taken together, the laccase based LBL biocatalytic NF membrane exhibits promising economic feasibility for MPs removal. The competitive NF performances, in terms of pure water permeability and salt rejection, as well as the MPs removal ability could be realized under a low pressure operation condition. This is a very important attribute of our developed membranes, especially in today's context, where energy-efficient water treatment processes are the main driver of membrane research. Moreover, sustainable BPA removal was demonstrated by rationally integrating backwashing into the NF process. Backwashing of our developed membrane can be simply carried out by using DI water, restoring up to >80% of the BPA removal ability after six cycles. This avoids the use of harsh chemical treatment, which not only help to protect the membrane, rendering a longer service duration, but also reduce the operation costs of the MPs removal process. With these features, the backwashing strategy could be suitable for other types of fouled NF membrane. In this concern, the detailed backwashing protocol and the bonding of separation layer with substrate of a certain NF membrane should be carefully considered.

However, it should be pointed out that backwashing is inadequate to further extend the lifespan of our designed biocatalytic NF membrane. As confirmed, the BPA removal efficiency, laccase activity as well as operation flux may hardly recovery to their original values after a 14-day filtration. Therefore, the regeneration of biocatalytic NF membrane is required. In this regard, Luo and coworkers proposed the effective regeneration protocols by immersing targeted biocatalytic membrane in NaSCN (1 M, pH 5) solution or NaOH (pH 10.6) solution with certain time [13]. Over 90% of both its original enzyme loading and specific activity were recovered. However, these chemicals with strong properties may swell the LBL components, which thoroughly damage the designed skin layer in this work. In the future research, we will dedicate our efforts to developing green and sustainable regeneration protocol for the LBL based biocatalytic NF membrane.

The design and fabrication of LBL based biocatalytic NF membrane for BPA removal was demonstrated in this work. A biocatalytic skin layer was successfully fabricated by synergistic laccase immobilization and LBL assembly on the lumen side of membrane support. PI immobilization strategy was confirmed as an effect approach for laccase immobilization, which endowed the LBL-PI biocatalytic NF membrane with desired NF performances under 2 bar pressure, competitive laccase loading (238.8 ± 3.5 μg/cm2), and laccase activity (0.6 U/cm2). It could be ascribed to the following features: (1) The PI process rationally integrated the formation of skin layer with immobilization of enzyme; (2) The natural conformation of enzyme was preserved with the PI process. For the BPA removal, LBL-PI membrane exhibited the ~79% removal efficiency under incubation mode. Under full recycling mode, the BPA removal efficiency could achieve 92.5% with the combined contribution of membrane rejection, adsorption and laccase catalysis of LBL-PI biocatalytic NF membrane. Moreover, the long-term reusability and stability of optimal membrane were also demonstrated by showing above 80% BPA removal efficiency for six cycles (14 days) with full recycling mode. This work clearly reveals the benefits of laccase-decorated LBL skin layer in MPs removal, and the resultant LBL based biocatalytic NF membrane therefore indicates its potential in purifying phenolic wastewater.
